articles.title: What can be done in the West Midlands to reduce risk of wildfires?
articles.summary: Politicians and firefighters discuss how we should tackle future wildfire risks.
articles.body:
A month on from the devastating fires that tore through the West Midlands on the hottest day of the year, communities are still reeling from what they have lost.

Dozens of homes across the region, including 19 in Stourbridge, were razed to the ground by the fires on 13 August.

Some people are living with their only surviving possessions in their car boot, while others stay in a caravan as they wait to be rehomed.

While action is needed to prevent a repeat of the wildfires, with more extreme temperatures on the horizon , what that should be is not yet clear.

Speaking to Politics Midlands , the West Midlands regional chair of the Fire Brigades Union (FBU), Martin Starkey, said the services in Staffordshire, where he works, were beyond stretched that day.

"Services in the Midlands on that day essentially ran out of resources and had to rely on brigades as far as London and Avon to come up and provide crews to help us cover the area," he said.

FBU statistics show that there were 20% fewer firefighters employed in 2025 compared to 2010.

The drop is even higher in the Midlands, with West Midlands Fire Service (WMFS) losing a quarter of its firefighters over this period, while Staffordshire Fire Service saw a drop of 27.2%.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who visited the scenes of devastation in Stourbridge , suggested that the country could follow the tactics of other countries and start using aeroplanes to fight large wildfires.

However, Starkey thinks that there should be more 4x4 capability within local fire services instead, as well as more firefighters put back on fire appliances and "better PPE, equipment and vehicles to help us deal with [the fires]".

Simon Tuhill, the chief fire officer at West Midlands Fire Service, told the BBC that in his role, he had no funding for capital in WMFS, which means things like new appliances and equipment.

During the fires, 19 smaller 4x4s were deployed, but Tuhill said they are reaching the end of their serviceable life.

"We need to think about more specialist vehicles that can respond to wildfires," he said.

Kerryn Little is a researcher in pyrogeography - the study of wildfires - at the University of Birmingham, and was also a volunteer firefighter in her home country of New Zealand.

"You can't just invest in response and suppression...We need to equally invest in prevention," she said.

For Little, this means managing landscapes from a fire risk perspective and developing early warning systems to communicate the risk of wildfires.

"The key thing is it's not just a one-off summer that we've seen," she said.

"Climate change is increasing the frequency and the intensity and duration of heat waves and droughts, these really hot, dry spells that drove the wildfires this year.

"So, essentially, climate change has loaded the dice for wildfire risk... we're going to have more days where a single spark will ignite a fire."

Tuhill and his crews know full well the impact of climate change.

"The fire service and my firefighters are at the front line of what climate change means to the United Kingdom," he told Politics Midlands.

This summer's prolonged heatwaves and dry vegetation led the prime minister to call the UK a "tinderbox", the same day the government sent a national alert to the country's mobile phones.

Ellie Chowns, the Green Party MP for North Herefordshire, believes we need to "supercharge efforts to transition to a clean, green economy" so we do not exacerbate the impact of climate change.

"The climate crisis is barrelling down the road towards us. We do absolutely have to adapt," she said.

Chowns believes the government does not yet have the urgency needed to address climate change.

"We've got to be more focused on preparedness and resilience across the board," she added.

Reform UK has backed away on net zero initiatives since taking control of local authorities across the country, calling off the climate emergency declarations made by councils such as Walsall and Newcastle-under-Lyme .

Such initiatives were introduced by previous administrations to include actions to reduce carbon emissions, protect biodiversity and help to build resilience against climate change.

Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice told Politics Midlands he was "delighted" that Newcastle-under-Lyme had "immediately scrapped the ridiculous net zero initiatives", claiming this had made savings of around £10m.

'Seeing fires destroying homes was like history repeating itself'

Midlands wildfire 999 calls were diverted to London

He has also defended comments he made saying people should enjoy the hotter weather, claiming that "the climate changes all the time" and that it was "smarter to adapt to climate change than to think you can stop it".

In response to hearing Tice's comments, Chowns told the BBC: "It's in our own interests, and frankly, it's in the interests not just of our children and grandchildren, it's in our interests now.

"Because the damage caused by climate change is going to hugely outweigh any possible cost that could be involved in transitioning to a more sustainable future."

Stourbridge falls under the authority of Dudley Council, whose leader, Conservative councillor Patrick Harley, said "a measured approach, not the extreme one" needed to be taken in regards to climate change.

"I think everyone agrees right across the political divide we have to adapt," he said.

Discussing the fires, Harley told the BBC that the emergency procedure put in place by the council "worked perfectly on the day", enabling collaboration with the emergency services.

"We've never seen anything like this before in the borough. And it's horrifying that you have a fire that can outrun a person and damage their property and cause the destruction that it caused."

Andy Burnham created the role of fire minister in response to this summers' wildfires.

Baroness Blake of Leeds's remit includes overseeing national emergency responses, fire policy and rescue operations.

It will also entail ensuring extreme weather preparations are in place across the country and the UK's resilience amid a rapidly changing climate.

Disposable barbecues are still banned from sale across the UK, a move that was due to most wildfires being caused by human behaviour.

While debates continue over what else should be done, Starkey has continued to be on the front line of the fires.

"What I can say, as a firefighter, is we are increasingly seeing hot summers, we are seeing the records get broken, we are seeing fire and rescue services stretched to their limits, running out of resources, running out of firefighters and struggling to deal with incidents," he said.

"I think history [has] shown that we don't learn ... So this year we need to make sure we learn these lessons."

articles.title: Richard Jupp on leaving Elbow and his recovery from addiction
articles.summary: Elbow's drummer Richard Jupp had everything... but still knew he was heading in the wrong direction.
articles.body:
Richard Jupp spent nearly 30 years of his life in Elbow.

From gigging in the pubs of Bury and Manchester to sell-out tours and winning international accolades, the drummer seemed to have everything a musician could ever want.

But underneath the surface the "myth of rock'n'roll" was not what it seemed.

"From the outside, I had everything you're supposed to want," he explaned.

"I was travelling the world, making records and living a life I'd dreamed about since I was a kid. We were at an extraordinary point in the band's career.

"But I asked myself 'What is any of that worth if I'm heading in a direction that was no longer working for me'?"

Now, after a decade of sobriety, Jupp is using his drumming to help others.

One of Manchester's most loved bands officially formed in Bury in 1990.

For Jupp, though, his ties go back as long as he can remember.

"I have actually known Pete the bass player since I was six months old," he said.

"We lived literally 250 yards from each other."

After growing up with bassist Pete Turner, the pair formed a band with guitarist Mark Potter at school.

They invited lead singer Guy Garvey to join them after meeting him at the former Stand College, just outside Bury, 36 years ago.

The four-piece were named Mr. Soft, later shortened to Soft soon became a five-piece when Mark's brother Craig joined them.

"It was the classic 10-year overnight success," Jupp said of the band which would come to be known in 1997 as Elbow's rise to fame.

"We'd always been hanging out, tinkering with music until it became our main focus.

"We saw everybody go off to uni, get jobs, go travelling. And we thought 'No - we're going to stick to this'."

After years of gigging, the band signed with Island Records after winning a Battle of the Bands competition.

After being dropped, Elbow later signed with V2 and released their debut album Asleep in the Back in 2001.

The album had been six years in the making.

Barely a year later, Elbow were playing at the Glastonbury Festival.

"We went from playing [before] 100 people to hearing 100,000 people clapping and cheering for you and singing along," Jupp said of those meteoric days.

"You're looking at the faces of the crowd and the people that you've created this thing with.

"And you would be like 'Oh My God - this is ridiculous'!"

Despite having made it to the big time, Jupp said he spent his career immersed in a music-industry culture in which drinking and drugs were completely normalised.

"I can only speak for my own experience - but it was kind of de rigueur.

"Less so now, but back in those days it was seen as some kind of rite of passage, it was normalised, and I did personally participate in that culture.

"I've witnessed within the industry, people who are still partaking - outside of the band - people who are still perpetuating that myth of rock'n'roll."

Jupp said he was able to separate the culture from his everyday life, and did not take drugs outside of touring with the band.

"It didn't ever come to point where it was outside of that," he said.

"It was sort of internalised from my point of view."

When he turned 40, Jupp said he decided the lifestyle was no longer working for him.

After about a year touring with the band while sober, Jupp said he made the decision to step down, formally leaving in 2016.

"It was starting to get to a point where I could see that there was a problem," he said.

Jupp said his decision had not been made lightly.

"Choosing sobriety and choosing recovery meant being prepared to walk away from a life that had given me fame, success and financial security," he said.

"It meant stepping away from an identity I'd carried for most of my adult life and accepting that my health, my family and my future had to come first."

Jupp said a big part of his decision to leave the band was wanting to do something different - and to spend more time with his family.

"In 2015 my son was diagnosed with autism - he was 13 or 14 at the time and that was just a paradigm shift for him," he explained.

"I had spent most of his little life here and then away and then here and then away.

"I just thought there are other things I want to do.

"I knew it would be a big move and a bold move.

"But it was very definitely the right move."

Since leaving the band, Jupp has been teaching drumming with a focus on the physical, cognitive and emotional benefits of the instrument - and has been sober throughout.

He holds sessions at his Manchester Drum Studio - as well was working at Liverpool Institute for Performing Arts (LIPA), teaching at dBs Institute Manchester and mentoring postgraduate students at Tileyard London.

"Since leaving the band, recovery has been one of the defining focuses of my life, and drumming has played a huge role in that," he said.

"Rhythm, repetition, movement and focus help bring me back into the moment.

"It is about sharing something that has genuinely helped me stay grounded and well.

"I know how significant that decision to choose recovery can be.

"Addiction is a disease and it's terrifying.

"And I was lucky enough to be able to make the decision of sobriety and be able to stand by it."

Jupp is taking his drumming workshop to Delamere Health clinic, an addiction rehabilitation centre in Cheshire, where he hopes to share with others the power of drumming, routine and rhythm.

"I know what it is to look at the life you are living and decide that something has to change," Judd said.

"So if I can now stand alongside people who are making that decision for themselves, particularly those just beginning their recovery, and offer something that might help them reconnect with themselves, their families or simply with life again that feels incredibly meaningful to me."

The clinic's founder Martin Preston, from south Manchester, said: "We're so looking forward to Richard coming in.

"What Rich is really passionate about is that recovery becomes quite a personal thing.

"So through drumming, Rich has found ways and means to regulate, to connect with others, to be mindful.

"It's the power of community, the power of the group coming together to share an experience."

articles.title: In 2001, Bear Grylls bought a remote Welsh island for £95,000; after four years rebuilding its only house, it now runs off-grid on wind, solar and harvested rainwater
articles.summary: UK News: In 2001, Bear Grylls bought a remote island off the coast of north Wales for £95,000. At the time, the island had just one house, which Grylls describ.
articles.body: In 2001, Bear Grylls bought a remote island off the coast of north Wales for £95,000. At the time, the island had just one house, which Grylls described as a “complete wreck”. He and his friends then spent four years rebuilding the property, turning the isolated place into a family retreat.The island is about six miles off the north Wales coast and is connected to a lighthouse, The Guardian reported. The house, which stands around 300ft above the sea, was once used by the lighthouse keeper’s family. Grylls said the location can become difficult in winter, when sea spray can reach over the roof.The property was bought as a place where Grylls could spend time away from the demands of his work. In a 2007 interview with The Guardian, he said the island had no telephone, emails or other people. His family would drive to a marina, load their food and other supplies into a RIB, and travel about six-and-a-half miles to the island.In a 2024 interview with National Geographic Traveller, he said his family owns “a little island” a few miles off the coast of north Wales that is “totally off-grid”. He said the house is powered by wind and solar, while rainwater is collected from the roof.A remote family retreatFor Grylls, the island is a place where he can spend time with his family without the schedules and meetings that are part of his working life.In the 2007 interview, he said his filming and work kept him away from his family for long periods. Even when he was at home, he often had meetings and a busy schedule.“What I find so hard about my work life and my filming life is that I'm away from my family so much,” Grylls said. “Even when I'm home it can be mad, with constant meetings, so what's so precious about this is that it's literally just us, no meetings, no nothing.”The family spent about six weeks on the island each summer. Getting there was part of the experience. They would travel from the marina by RIB with food, the children and everything else they needed for their stay.Once there, their days were centred around outdoor activities and family time. Grylls said they would swim, climb, use hammocks, have barbecues and take shelter in the house when the weather turned wet.Wind, solar power and rainwaterThe island’s remote location means that the property operates differently from an ordinary home. In his 2024 National Geographic Traveller interview, Grylls explained that the house uses wind and solar power.“My family owns a little island a few miles off the coast off North Wales that’s totally off-grid,” he said. “The house is powered by wind and solar; we even collect rainwater off the roof.”Being off-grid also fits the kind of environment Grylls values. He said the island can sometimes feel isolating, but that is part of what he likes about it.“It can be isolating sometimes, but I love that,” he said. “I spend so much of my year around people and I’m not a natural extrovert. I need a little quiet time to sit and recharge.”The island also gives his family access to the surrounding coast. Grylls previously described the area as having sea cliffs, dolphins and seals. The family used their boat for trips along the coast, water-skiing and travelling back to the mainland.A place for adventureThe island’s surroundings have also allowed Grylls to share his interest in outdoor activities with his children.In the 2007 interview, he said his son Jesse had been interested in activities such as skydiving, camping and climbing from a young age. Grylls said they climbed together and that he had also taken Jesse paragliding.The family also explored the coast around the island, using the boat to find coves for picnics. Grylls said the area was largely National Trust land.For someone whose career has centred on adventure, the setting offered many of the activities associated with his television work. articles.title: At 100, Atlanta's Barbara Haig still drives her white Ford Mustang; she says caution, not age, will determine how long she stays behind the wheel
articles.summary: US News: At an age when many people are content to slow down, Barbara Haig is still putting the top down and heading out in her white Ford Mustang. According t.
articles.body: At an age when many people are content to slow down, Barbara Haig is still putting the top down and heading out in her white Ford Mustang. According to a news report by 11alive website, Haig turned 100 on August 28, but the milestone has done little to change the rhythm of a life built around curiosity, faith, travel and independence. Just two weeks after reaching a century, she was still driving around her Atlanta community, teaching Sunday school and volunteering. For Haig, getting older has never meant giving up on the things that make life interesting.A lifetime of seeing the worldTravel has been one of the defining threads of Haig's life. For decades, she explored the United States and the world with a close friend she met through church. Together, they visited all 50 states, all seven continents and more than 75 countries. Their adventures took them from the fjords of Norway to China and Russia, destinations that offered experiences far removed from what they knew at home. She also traveled to Cambodia, where she rode an elephant, and visited the Holy Land.Her friend died about two decades ago, but Haig did not stop traveling. The desire to see new places continued long after she began making those journeys on her own.She never stopped trying new thingsHaig's adventurous streak was not limited to airports and passports. She took up water skiing in her 60s and continued the sport well into her 90s, eventually stopping at 94 after her cardiologist advised her to give it up. A heart valve replacement has since become another chapter in a life that has included plenty of challenges without allowing them to define her. Today, she remains active in her church and community. Haig has been a member of Second Ponce de Leon Baptist Church since 1960 and continues to teach Sunday school. She also volunteers three days a week with Care for Caregivers, a respite-care ministry that helps families looking after loved ones.Haig and the MustangHaig has been fond of convertibles for years. After giving them up for a period, seeing other drivers enjoying the spring weather with their tops down convinced her that she was ready for another one. The white Mustang became her latest companion on the road, states the news report. At 100, Haig remains conscious of the responsibilities that come with driving. She avoids getting behind the wheel at night, follows traffic rules and takes a cautious approach, even though she remains comfortable driving on interstate highways. Family members and friends also keep an eye on her, checking in regularly to make sure she is doing well. Her philosophy is straightforward: age alone does not have to determine when an activity ends. Judgment, caution and the ability to do something safely matter more.One careful mile at a timeHaig does not appear interested in treating 100 as a finish line. Her life has been shaped by a willingness to explore, whether that meant skiing across a lake, traveling to the far corners of the world or simply climbing into a convertible for a drive around Atlanta. There is no elaborate formula behind her longevity. Instead, her approach seems rooted in staying curious, remaining useful and refusing to spend too much time worrying about circumstances she cannot control.At 100, Barbara Haig is still looking ahead. For now, that means another Sunday school lesson, another volunteer shift and another careful drive in her Mustang, with plenty of road still left to explore.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Mystery son and disputed heir: Uganda’s king buried amid succession dispute
articles.summary: The 34-year-old monarch’s death has opened a rare challenge to the traditional process of choosing Tooro’s next king.
articles.body:
Fort Portal, Uganda – When King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV of Tooro was buried on September 12, the ceremony unfolded under the shadow of a bitter dispute over who should succeed him.

Prince Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, a 56-year-old news anchor and editor at Uganda Broadcasting Corporation, had been selected by the royal clan to succeed Oyo. During the burial at the Karambi Royal Tombs in Fort Portal, he formally assumed power by casting nine coffee berries into the king’s grave, part of the traditional handover ritual.

Oyo’s mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa, and his sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale, have opposed Kijanangoma’s selection, saying the late king’s will named a son as his heir.

Oyo never married and was not publicly known to have children. After his death, Tooro’s Prime Minister Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki announced that the king had left a son whose identity would be revealed at an appropriate time. The child has not been publicly identified.

Oyo’s family says a 2022 will named a son whom he described as his lawfully recognised biological son as heir to the throne. But Babiito clan elders, who are responsible for guarding the Tooro royal lineage, determining succession and safeguarding the kingdom’s traditions, say Oyo had not introduced the child through the customary process and instead backed Kijanangoma as his successor.

“The will is not a determinant of who is supposed to be a king; it is a document that expresses one’s wish,” said Reverend Father Charles Oyo, a Babiito clan elder. “The Musuuga [Babiito clan leader] is above the will.”

Princess Komuntale has accused the elders of trying to take over the throne.

“King Oyo was a very peaceful man, a very humble man,” she said. “I just don’t want these evil vultures to come and steal what he worked so hard for. I continue to stand with my brother.”

The dispute has divided opinion over who should be regarded as Oyo’s legitimate successor. The Ugandan government also became involved in talks aimed at resolving the dispute before the burial.

Oyo’s own path to the throne began when he was just three years old.

He became king in 1995 after the death of his father, Patrick David Matthew Kaboyo Olimi III, and was recognised as the world’s youngest reigning monarch.

As a child, Oyo was homeschooled, with the palace serving as his classroom. When he later joined primary school, childhood friends remember him as a kind and warm person.

During school holidays, he sometimes sneaked out of the family’s private residence in Buziga, Kampala, to play football in the neighbourhood.

Martin Odong, a radio journalist and childhood friend, remembers him as “friendly, social and compassionate”.

Oyo would stop football games to check on an injured player, regardless of which side they were playing for, Odong said.

His love of football continued into adulthood. He promoted local tournaments, including the Tooro Kingdom MTN Masaza Cup, which was suspended as his health deteriorated.

Oyo died on August 27, aged 34, in the United States while receiving cancer treatment. His body was returned to Uganda for nine days of mourning before his burial at the Karambi Royal Tombs, which coincided with Empango, the anniversary of his coronation.

At St John’s Cathedral, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa remembered her son as someone who had always protected her.

“He was my shield who always stood for me,” she said.

She recalled praying for his life when she was in hospital.

“When I was in the hospital, I said, ‘God, please leave my son alone; take me first,’” she said. “He [God] decided to take him [King Oyo] first. I said, ‘Why? Because he was closer to You than me.’”

Princess Komuntale described her brother as a “funny person” who “always brightened my day”.

Although he was younger than her, she said, he often behaved like the older sibling and protected her and their mother after their father “left to be with the Lord”.

Father Charles Oyo remembered him as a “handsome king who loved his kingdom so much”.

He said Oyo died just as he was “beginning to demonstrate his abilities and capacity as a king”.

Uganda is a constitutional republic, and its traditional kings have no formal political authority. But the kingdoms retain cultural influence and command loyalty among many of their communities.

Uganda abolished its traditional kingdoms in 1967. They were restored in 1993 under President Yoweri Museveni.

Oyo was guided by regents while he was a child and took on the full responsibilities of the monarchy as an adult.

His unusual position meant he met presidents, royalty and other world leaders from a young age. Among them was former South African President Nelson Mandela, who reportedly wanted to meet the young king during a visit to Uganda. Oyo, however, was more interested in playing with his toys behind the VIP tent.

As an adult, he used the platform of the throne to promote issues beyond the kingdom.

In 2020, he climbed the Rwenzori Mountains to draw attention to climate change and the retreat of the glaciers there.

He also supported a campaign to plant 10 million trees across Tooro over five years.

He promoted healthy living and took part in cancer awareness runs. Komuntale called him her “best workout partner”.

Before his death, Oyo had allocated land and begun fundraising for a paediatric hospital in Kyenjojo district. Clan elders have since appealed to the government to complete the project and establish a specialised cancer facility and an international stadium in his memory.

According to his sister, he began experiencing pain in his back and rib cage last year. The family initially thought it might be linked to strenuous exercise or ulcers.

He later travelled to Kenya, where he was diagnosed with angiosarcoma, an aggressive form of cancer, before travelling to Germany for treatment and eventually to the US.

“He told us to keep it private, and we respected that,” Komuntale said.

She said that shortly before his death, Oyo spoke to key workers in Uganda about returning home. He wanted to celebrate Empango, the anniversary of his coronation, with his people.

For Komuntale, the king remained her younger brother even after he became one of Africa’s most recognisable traditional rulers.

She remembered playing dodgeball with him and his love for his three dogs.

“Even though you were crowned a king, you were still a kid who loved to play,” she said.

“I will keep your legacy, what you loved, and we will talk about you every day.”

But in 2026, the pattern changed.On September 8, UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband used some of the British government's strongest language yet on Israel's occupation, telling the House of Commons that Palestinians in parts of the West Bank were being driven from their homes and land in what Britain now considers "ethnic cleansing" carried out by "settler terrorists".The groundshaking statement was Despite this visual evidence and Netanyahu's assurance, the Israeli police has made zero arrests in connection with the violence.That contradiction captures Israel's current position: public condemnation of violent "rogue" settlers while powerful elements of the government continue policies that expand settlement territory.The E1 AreaThe most strategically significant development of 2025 was the final approval in August by the Higher Planning Council of plans to build 3,401 housing units in E1, followed by the publication of construction tenders in December 2025.After years during which successive Israeli governments refrained from advancing E1 due to sustained international and American pressure, the Netanyahu-Smotrich government approved the E1 plans. These plans are universally regarded as among the most damaging possible settlement decisions for the prospects of peace and a two-state outcome.The E1 area sits at the geographic heart of the West Bank.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Development of this area as an Israeli settlement would split the West Bank into two non-contiguous parts, cutting the territorial link between the northern and southern West Bank, and preclude the development of a Palestinian metropolitan area connecting Ramallah, East Jerusalem, and Bethlehem.It would also effectively consolidate the annexation of Ma'ale Adumim into the Israeli urban space.In September 2025, Netanyahu signed an agreement for accelerated development with the Municipality of Ma'ale Adumim, committing the government to invest 3 billion shekels in infrastructure for the E1 settlement and for the development of Ma'ale Adumim.These commitments signal that E1 is no longer merely a planning approval but an active construction project.Trump's reaction to Israeli settler 'terrorists'US president Donald Trump's record is far more complicated than a simple pro- or anti-settlement label.During his first presidency, the US moved away from the long-standing American position that Israeli settlements violated international law. It’s an act of terrorIn October 2025, he said Israel was “not going to do anything” with the West Bank after the Knesset advanced an annexation measure.In 2026, Washington’s position has become more interventionist again. US Ambassador Mike Huckabee has publicly described violent settlers as terrorists, and in September he travelled to Turmus Ayya to meet Palestinian Americans affected by settler attacks. Reuters reported growing US pressure on Netanyahu to confront settler violence.What the UN says UN Security Council Resolution 2334, adopted in 2016, reaffirmed that Israeli settlements in territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem, have “no legal validity” and constitute a major obstacle to peace. The council demanded an end to settlement activity.In July 2024, the International Court of Justice went further. Its advisory opinion concluded that Israel’s continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory is unlawful and said Israel must end new settlement activity, evacuate settlers and provide reparation for damage caused by its unlawful acts.The UN General Assembly has continued to reaffirm the same position.In December 2025, it adopted a resolution on Israeli settlements by 146 votes to 13, condemning settlement activity, land confiscation, forced transfer and violence against Palestinian civilians and calling for accountability for extremist settlers. The United States voted against the resolution alongside Israel.In June 2026, the UN secretary-general’s report again said settlement activity was continuing and recorded thousands of newly advanced or approved housing units.Israel has rejected all such opinions.A new phase of the conflictTha larger global consensus is that the West Bank crisis is no longer simply about individual extremist settlers burning fields or attacking Palestinian villagers.The evidence points to a much larger transformation: a growing settler population; hundreds of outposts; expanding roads and infrastructure; recurring violence; demolitions; forced evictions; loss of agricultural access; and the displacement of entire communities.The Netanyahu coalition includes ministers such as Bezalel Smotrich, who has openly advocated extending Israeli sovereignty over the West Bank. In 2025, Smotrich told the Knesset that Israel should move toward applying sovereignty in Judea and Samaria and described the policy as a process of establishing "de facto sovereignty".The UN's assessment is therefore less about whether every Israeli official orders every settler attack and more about the cumulative effect of policies, enforcement failures, settlement expansion and land control.Its March 2026 report said settler violence continued in a coordinated and largely unchallenged manner, with Israeli authorities playing a central role in directing, participating in or enabling aspects of the conduct.That is why the language coming from Britain and other Western governments in 2026 has become so severe. London is no longer talking only about isolated violations. It is arguing that the cumulative process amounts to "ethnic cleansing" and that Israel's continued occupation itself is unlawful.Whether that pressure can actually change events on the ground remains uncertain.Till then, Israel continues to expand settlements, Palestinians continue to lose access to land, and Washington remains unwilling to impose the kind of sanctions used by Britain and other Western governments.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2018, Cartier’s parent company disclosed destroying nearly €500 million of luxury watches; it bought them back to prevent heavy discounts from weakening its brands
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Richemont, the parent company of Cartier, destroyed nearly €500 million in unsold luxury watches to protect brand value and maintain exclusivity in the market. Understand the impact of inventory management on luxury pricing and consumer perception.
articles.body: Luxury watches rely on a simple idea: scarcity can be part of the product itself. A timepiece may contain intricate mechanical components and expensive materials, but its value can also depend on where it is sold, how widely it is available and how consistently its price is maintained. For the companies behind brands such as Cartier, allowing large quantities of unsold watches to circulate at deep discounts could therefore create a problem that went beyond excess stock.According to Richemont's 2018 annual report, the Swiss luxury group behind Cartier carried out exceptional watch inventory buy-backs worth €203 million in the year to March 2018, following €278 million in the previous year. The two rounds totalled about €481 million and were aimed at reducing excess stock held by multi-brand retail partners and bringing inventories closer to end-client demand. Richemont's move came as it sought to prevent unsold watches from entering unauthorised channels, where they could be offered at lower prices.When unsold watches became a problemThe stock buildup was linked to a slowdown in luxury demand and a build-up of inventory among retailers. Some dealers had held watches for years without finding buyers, leaving them with an incentive to clear the products through unofficial channels. The situation became particularly visible in Asian markets, where changing consumer behaviour and China's anti-corruption campaign had contributed to weaker demand for some luxury goods. Richemont's 2018 annual report also states that the group had undertaken exceptional inventory buy-backs to address this excess stock. Rather than allowing retailers to reduce prices sharply, the company purchased watches back from them. This gave retailers a way to clear their inventories while allowing Richemont to regain control of products carrying its brands before they reached the grey market. The issue was not that the watches were defective. They were legitimate luxury products that had become difficult to sell through the authorised retail network at their intended prices. Once watches entered the grey market, they could appear alongside authorised products at considerably lower prices, making the difference visible to consumers.The cost of protecting a luxury priceResearch published in the Journal of Business Research has examined how consumers perceive luxury goods when price, rarity and status are closely connected. The findings help explain why discounting can have consequences beyond the immediate loss in revenue: for some luxury consumers, high prices and limited availability can contribute to perceptions of exclusivity.The grey market creates an additional challenge because manufacturers have less control over how their products are priced and presented once they leave authorised channels. Research published in Transportation Research Part E has examined grey-market activity in luxury supply chains and highlighted the difficulty manufacturers face in managing prices and distribution when products move through unauthorised markets. For Richemont, getting rid of the surplus watches was thus a way of safeguarding the pricing system associated with its brands. They did not have to sell the unwanted inventory at increasingly lower prices, while retailers could reduce their inventories without flooding the market with discounted merchandise.Why destroying the watches made senseHowever, the value of the brand names was what was considered during the calculation, not the potential value of each watch. In 2018, The Guardian reported that Richemont had been destroying watches after buying them back from retailers as the group dealt with excess inventory. By then, the company had begun to bring its stock levels under control, and Richemont indicated that the exceptional buy-back programme was coming to an end.The episode showed how differently luxury firms handle unsold products. In other sectors, excess supply is handled via discounts and sales or different distribution channels. However, for a luxury watch company, a significantly discounted watch can have negative effects on the value proposition of that watch itself. articles.title: In 2016, WFP helped Sahrawi refugees grow barley without soil in the Sahara; hydroponic trays produced fresh animal feed in seven days while using 90% less water
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2016, the World Food Programme introduced innovative hydroponics to empower Sahrawi refugees in the Sahara with soil-free barley cultivation, drastically improving animal feed production and saving water.
articles.body: Tens of thousands of Sahrawi refugees living in camps close to Tindouf in southwest Algeria face severe constraints on growing food. The arid environment provides little agricultural land or water, while families depend heavily on livestock such as goats and camels for food and income. In 2016, Sahrawi agricultural engineer Taleb Brahim began experimenting with hydroponics after seeing how the technique could grow fresh fodder with little water. In March 2017, he presented the idea to the World Food Programme's Innovation Accelerator, which selected it for further development. WFP staff in Algeria then worked with Brahim, the Innovation Accelerator, and Oxfam to develop and test low-tech hydroponic units built with locally available materials. Rethinking nearly every tenet of traditional farming was necessary to get that system to function consistently in desert environments.Barley cultivation without soilHydroponics is especially useful in areas with poor, nonexistent, or simply too salty soil to produce crops since it enables plants to grow with their roots hanging directly in nutrient-enriched water rather than planted in the ground. Barley seeds were spread across shallow trays and kept moist inside simple units built from locally available materials. The systems could be powered by solar energy and required only a water pump, making them considerably simpler than the high-tech hydroponic equipment first tested. The World Food Programme's own project overview notes that this method needs about ninety per cent less water than traditional soil-based agriculture, since the water feeding the trays can be captured and reused rather than lost to dry desert soil. Within about seven days, the barley in each tray sprouted into a dense mat of fresh green fodder ready to be fed straight to animals, cutting what would normally be a growing season for a fully mature grain crop down to little more than a week for usable feed. That speed turned out to matter just as much as the water savings once the trays reached the camps themselves.Feeding animals within a weekBefore the hydroponic units came, household scraps and whatever the animals could forage were usually the best refugees could do for feed, and the lean, unproductive condition of many herds showed it. Families who adopted the trays reported an improvement within months, with notably increased milk and meat production after their goats and camels had regular access to fresh green feed rather than dried trash.A Sahrawi participant named Maryam said her community still could not quite believe they now had fodder growing right there in the camp. The technique also took significantly less work than attempting to farm in open desert soil, as a family could manage a few trays inside a shaded building, without requiring vast tracts of land or heavy irrigation equipment. As the approach proved successful in the camps, WFP and its partners began adapting the technology for other locations.Taking the idea beyond the Sahara DesertWithin a few years of the first trial, identical hydroponic fodder units had been installed in refugee situations in Chad and Jordan, each time slightly customised to local conditions but built around the same core idea of growing more food with significantly less water. Research partners such as the Fraunhofer Institute later worked on expanding the concept beyond animal fodder toward vegetables like lettuce and herbs, aiming to stretch the same low-water approach further into human diets rather than just livestock feed. For populations in some of the driest and most unstable places in the world, the appeal of a system that requires no soil, uses up to 90% less water and produces useful fodder within days is clear.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: World's Oldest Message: In 1906, a British biologist released 1,020 weighted bottles with messages to map North Sea currents; 55% returned quickly, while one resurfaced 108 years later
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In an incredible tale of persistence and ocean currents, a glass bottle released in 1906 finally returns after 108 years, uncovering a historic scientific experiment by biologist George Parker Bidder. Discover how this experiment mapped North Sea currents and more.
articles.body: Before the invention of satellites and floating sensor buoys, scientists had only two tools to comprehend the true movement of ocean water: patience and a willingness to let the sea do the work. Although fishermen were already aware that currents moved objects in somewhat predictable patterns, no one had sufficient evidence to precisely map those movements. Using nothing more complex than glass bottles and a small monetary prize, a British marine biologist concluded at the beginning of the twentieth century that the easiest way to answer the question was to give the task to the fishing fleets themselves.George Parker Bidder, a Marine Biological Association researcher with a lifelong interest in the mechanics of the seabed and the water flowing above it, was that biologist. He launched 1,020 weighted bottles into the North Sea from a research vessel between 1904 and 1906. Each bottle had a printed postcard that asked the person who found it to record the date and place before returning it to Plymouth. Knowing why Bidder weighed his bottles instead of just allowing them to float on the surface helps to clarify why the experiment was valuable from a scientific standpoint.Creating bottles that followed the seabedTo replicate deep water movement rather than the more erratic drift patterns near the surface, Bidder's containers, which he named bottom trailers, were designed to dip near the seabed while being maintained slightly above it by a short length of rigid wire. This distinction was significant since the bottles were most likely to be caught by trawlers running their nets along the bottom, providing Bidder with an army of citizen scientists dispersed throughout the North Sea fishing towns. Archival records describe how Bidder designed and refined the bottom-trailer bottles so they could remain near the seabed and survive extended periods in the North Sea. Over the next few years, the results that came back provided Bidder with exactly the kind of trend he had anticipated finding.When the bottles returned Fishermen who found a bottle and sent back the filled-out postcard received a little prize, and the inducement worked well enough that the bidder recorded a return rate of some fifty-five per cent for the entire set distributed. By comparing the original dropping points of each bottle with where they turned up, he was able to plot a clear and consistent east-to-west flow in the deep water current through the southern North Sea. This helped later researchers understand how pollutants, larvae and nutrients move along the seabed rather than just floating near the surface. Decades later, Bidder became president of the Marine Biological Association, which made what happened next seem almost like providence rather than chance. While most of the thousand or so bottles were finally accounted for, a handful seemed to have disappeared into the water forever, at least until one popped up in a spot no one was expecting.The bottle that outlived them allMarianne Winkler, a retired postal worker from Germany, was walking on a beach on Germany’s Amrum Island in 2015 when she saw an ancient glass bottle with a card inside telling her to crack it open. At last she and her husband dug up a postcard, printed in English, German and Dutch, addressed to a Mr Bidder of an association she had never heard of, and despatched it back just as ordered.Association staff were surprised to receive a response to an experiment that had finished more than a century earlier. When it was determined that the bottle’s release date was 30 November 1906, Guinness World Records verified the oldest message in a bottle ever found, after the bottle spent 108 years and 138 days at sea before washing ashore.The association sent Winkler an old English shilling in the mail, fulfilling the promise on the card, paying a debt that, technically, had been owed since before either of Bidder's own grandchildren were born. The bottle, along with the nearly four hundred others from Bidder’s original set that were never recovered, remains one of the more fascinating examples of how a piece of straightforward scientific fieldwork may silently keep working long after everyone engaged in constructing it has passed away.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Voting under way in Sweden election that could see far right in government
articles.summary: The far-right Sweden Democrats party could enter government for the first time if right-wing bloc wins.
articles.body:
Voters in Sweden are heading to the polls in an extremely close general election that will see either the far right enter government for the first time or the centre-left opposition reclaim power.

Opposition leader Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats was among the first to cast her ballot after polling stations opened at 8:00am (06:00 GMT) on Sunday.

The 59-year-old, who in 2021 became the first woman to serve as Sweden’s prime minister, voted with her husband at a school in her home municipality of Nacka, south of Stockholm.

Pre-election opinion polls have long credited the four parties in her left-wing bloc with a comfortable lead over conservative Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s four-party alliance, which includes the far-right Sweden Democrats.

But the gap narrowed significantly in the final days of the campaign.

“It is now up to the Swedish people to decide which direction our country should take. Should we have a government entirely dominated by the Sweden Democrats? Something that has never happened in Sweden before? Or should we have a government led by me, which will steer Sweden in a new spirit of cooperation?” Andersson told reporters after voting.

Her party has pledged to boost the welfare state and help struggling households cope with the rising cost of living.

Outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson is seeking a second four-year term at the helm of the European Union nation.

He has led Sweden since 2022 with a three-party centre-right coalition. It relies on outside support from the Sweden Democrats, an anti-immigration, far-right party that has moved towards the political mainstream, for a parliamentary majority.

If the right-wing bloc is re-elected, the Sweden Democrats can expect Cabinet posts in the next government.

Kristersson has promised to focus on improving Swedes’ everyday lives, following his government’s clampdown on organised crime and immigration.

“We want to use our new and far better preconditions to improve the lives of ordinary people … to make Sweden great again,” Kristersson told news agency AFP before the vote.

The Sweden Democrats , a party with neo-Nazi roots, took 20.5 percent of the vote in the 2022 election to become the biggest party on the right.

Kristersson announced in April that his conservative Moderates would allow the party into government if the right has a majority – though he would remain prime minister even if the Sweden Democrats are the stronger party.

Voting stations close at 8:00pm (18:00 GMT) when exit polls are expected to be published, with the first reliable results expected several hours later.

Some eight million people are eligible to vote in the election, in a country of 10.6 million where voter turnout regularly tops 80 percent.

About half of voters have cast their ballots in advance.

articles.title: “Where were you for a month?”: Bihar flood-hit woman's blunt question to leaders goes viral
articles.summary: A video has drawn widespread attention after a flood-affected woman from Bihar used it to call out the state's political leadership over what she desc.
articles.body: A video has drawn widespread attention after a flood-affected woman from Bihar used it to call out the state's political leadership over what she describes as a complete absence of support during nearly a month of flooding in her village. In the video, shared by theindiaonfeedofficial she says her community has been battling floodwaters for almost a month, and the situation has steadily worsened rather than improved. According to the account in the video, the floods swept away essential household supplies, including atta (wheat flour), cooking oil, and vegetables, leaving families in her village struggling to even prepare a basic meal. She says that throughout this entire period, not a single local pradhan, councillor, MLA, MP, or any other authority figure visited the village to check on residents or offer assistance.A direct message to the Chief MinisterWhat makes the video particularly pointed is that she addresses it directly to Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary, saying she is recording it specifically to bring her village's situation to his attention, since no one else appears to have taken notice. Samrat Choudhary took charge as Bihar's Chief Minister in April 2026, succeeding long-time CM Nitish Kumar, making him the state's current top administrative authority during this flood crisis. Toward the end of the video, she also issues a sharp warning to politicians in general, saying that if they come looking for votes when elections roll around, villagers like her will not forget how they were abandoned during this crisis. It's a line that captures a sentiment increasingly visible in flood-hit parts of Bihar this year: frustration not just with the disaster itself, but with what many residents feel is a pattern of political neglect until it's politically convenient to show up.Part of a wider pattern this flood seasonThis video does not appear to be an isolated case. Bihar has been dealing with a serious flood crisis through August and September 2026, with the Ganga and its tributaries submerging villages across multiple districts. Several other similar incidents have surfaced on social media around the same time. In Maner, a village known locally as the "village of soldiers", Ratan Tola was left submerged with local reports noting that neither the area's MP nor MLA had visited to check on residents. In Katihar, a Congress MP's flood-relief visit itself turned controversial after he was seen being carried piggyback by villagers through waterlogged terrain, sparking political sparring over whether the optics reflected poor planning or simple necessity given his health. Purnia MP Pappu Yadav was separately seen getting stranded himself while attempting to reach flood victims in a low-lying river region. Taken together, these incidents point to a broader, more strained relationship this flood season between affected communities and the political representatives meant to be helping them, of which this woman's video appears to be the latest and one of the more directly worded examples.Why this video is resonatingVideos like this tend to go viral precisely because they put a human face and voice to frustrations that are otherwise reported only in numbers, districts affected, people evacuated, and relief camps set up. Her testimony, if verified, reflects concerns that flood relief in parts of rural Bihar remains inconsistent, with visible administrative response sometimes arriving only after public pressure builds online. It's worth noting that this account comes directly from a self-recorded social media video, and at the time of writing, it does not appear to have been independently corroborated by mainstream news outlets, nor has the Bihar government or CM Samrat Choudhary's office issued any specific public response to this particular video. As with many such viral clips during disaster situations, the core claims, the extent of the flooding, the exact duration, and whether any officials visited before or after the video went viral, would benefit from direct verification by ground reporters or an official statement.A larger question, beyond one videoWhether or not this specific incident receives an official response, it adds to a growing chorus of similar complaints emerging from Bihar's flood-hit regions this season. For residents like the woman in this video, the question isn't just about one missed visit; it's about whether disaster response reaches people when they need it, rather than only after their frustration becomes impossible to ignore online.Note: This article is based on claims made directly in the woman's self-recorded video. At the time of writing, these specific claims had not been independently verified by a mainstream news outlet, and no official response from the Bihar government had been issued regarding this particular video.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: 'Forget Notting Hill - we set our new romcom in the east end of Glasgow'
articles.summary: Romantic comedy Premature is out in cinemas next Friday, despite a microscopic budget.
articles.body:
Film fans have had plenty of chances to spot Glasgow on the big screen in recent years, from superhero blockbusters to futuristic sci-fi thrillers.

Now the city is to star in cinemas once again - but the difference is that it won't be doubling for another location. It is actually set in the city.

Romantic comedy Premature is out in cinemas next Friday, despite a microscopic budget that is the fraction of Hollywood productions like Spider-Man: Brand New Day .

The indie film - by writer and director Kevin Walls - was shot across the city, meaning landmarks such as Kelvingrove Art Gallery pop up - a well as the less obvious location of an east end flat.

The film stars James Rottger and Elle Watson as Cameron and Eilidh - mismatched flatmates who face the prospect of parenthood after a one-night stand.

"We shot quite a bit in a flat in the east end, maybe about nine days there," Walls said.

"There is a key scene we did in a close there. It is not necessarily the most romantic location you would think of for a romcom, but in real life that's exactly where these things happen.

"Why can't we set a romcom in a flat in the east end? It looks really beautiful on the big screen."

That vibe is something the film's leading lady agrees with, despite Glasgow's film appearances often being due to it looking Gothic .

"We are so used to Glasgow being this dark and gritty place, but that's not reflective of the city overall", Watson said.

"It's great having it on screen as a bright and funny place, with people falling in love there. Shooting in locations I've grown up around was great too, as I've been going to Kelvingrove since I was a little kid.

"Part of me wanted to run around the building when it was all quiet. But when you see it on the screen it looks beautiful. Being from Glasgow you are so used to it that you almost become immune to the spectacle of the building, and how grand it is."

Walls admitted to BBC Scotland News that some of the choices were made through necessity.

"The locations were tricky because we didn't have any money," she said. "So we were begging – I'd usually go down and speak to people about what I was trying to do. I explained I wasn't going to tear up their space or anything like that."

Premature is the first feature film Kevin has directed, having worked on short films and adverts in the past.

He has also juggled other jobs, including lecturing and editing highlights of football matches for YouTube channels, with money raised going back into Premature.

A Kickstarter campaign helped secure funding needed for a cinema release.

"Cinema-going is really important to me, and through sheer determination I was going to get this on a cinema screen too, as it deserves to be seen there", Walls said.

Watson's character Eilidh harbours dreams of being an artist, but is frustrated that life is not going to plan. Her flatmate Cameron is meticulous and career driven, but everything changes for both of them when they drunkenly sleep together.

"This whole film is about two people being chucked out of any sense of control they thought they had," said James Rottger, who plays the leading man.

"Particularly for Cameron, that's the point of the film – I leaned into the bit of me that's a control freak and likes to do things a certain way, and then brought that out in the character."

Like his co-star, he was delighted to see so much of Glasgow on screen, and being presented in a bright light.

"It's brilliant big productions are coming here and using Glasgow as a double, but it's important we see Scotland on the big screen as itself," he said.

"The film Kevin has written shows Glasgow in a warm light, literally and figuratively. The red sandstone flats, Kelvingrove, the pubs – it's all there."

Premature marks Scotstoun native Watson's big screen debut, after mostly working in theatre and short films or adverts.

Unlike his co-star, Rottger has a fair number of screen credits, including roles in Gary: Tank Commander and a couple of rom-coms regarded as a bit cheesy - Irish Wish with Lindsay Lohan and festive TV film A Hot Cocoa Christmas.

However, for this film both stars say they could relate to their characters.

"I'm probably closer to where Cameron ends up than where he starts off," said Rottger, who has two young daughters.

"As a dad waiting for a baby to be born, you are out of having any control. The nerves you feel knowing you will be a parent is terrifying for the first time."

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

For Watson, the relatability came in a different way.

"Any woman in her late 20s or 30s will have thought about children, it's omnipresent," she said.

"You feel you need to be confident about your choice as it will soon be taken away from you as you get older.

"But it was important the film is not just about Eilidh being pregnant – it's using that for her to discover who she is and what she wants from life."

Walls admits he had to overcome his own doubts during the creative process, having put so much effort in.

"There were so many times you'd think 'what am I doing here, this is a terrible idea and won't work' – I had to push past that and be confident," he said.

Seeing the finished product in cinemas will make it all worth it though, as Watson sums up.

"It feels like a miracle for this film with a tiny budget and a hope and a prayer, to be on the big screen."

articles.title: Ashford Odeon restoration plans revealed
articles.summary: People are being asked to give their thoughts on plans on for the cinema, which was built in 1936.
articles.body:
New designs have revealed how Ashford's former Odeon cinema could look once it has been restored.

The cinema was built in 1936 but has been empty since 2018, last being used by Mecca Bingo. Now, Ashford Borough Council says plans to bring it back to life are one step closer.

Those plans include a new performance space, a cafe/bar with an "informal workspace", and a gallery. The building's ballroom will also be restored and would be available for hire.

The public can view the plans at a consultation event on 18 September, between 10:00 and 16:00 BST, at County Square shopping centre.

A spokesperson for the council said: "The project responds to the community's strong call for more arts, cultural and performance space in Ashford town centre."

The authority said the new designs were developed based on feedback from the community and "local cultural partners".

Changes on the initial plans, it said, included increased capacity for the studio theatre, an improved backstage area and a more accessible High Street entrance and box office.

A planning application will be submitted after the public consultation event.

articles.title: What's next after Donald Trump's united Ireland comments?
articles.summary: At a press conference on Saturday, the US president said he would "love to see" a united Ireland.
articles.body:
Nothing is out of bounds in the unpredictable world of Donald Trump.

Even the most sensitive of political issues is considered fair game by the US president.

So should we be surprised when he strays on to the political minefield of Irish unity and declares his full-throated support for reunification?

Well yes, because prior to his declaration on Saturday , President Trump avoided any tricky questions around Irish unity.

He has talked about a "merger" in the past but stopped short of expressing his personal opinion often referencing the complicated relationships.

But all that changed on Saturday when, sitting alongside Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin, he predicted a united Ireland will happen and he will "love to see it".

But far from being a classic off the cuff Trump intervention, it appears he discussed Irish unity with President Connolly and the taoiseach during their meetings.

It may have been a Trump tactic to put his hosts at ease and to avoid more trickier conversations around Gaza and the costly fall out of his war with Iran.

Or maybe his plan was to talk up Irish reunification to bolster support with Irish Americans voters ahead of the mid term elections.

Whatever his intentions the fall out has stirred a political whirlwind.

President Trump started to feel it yesterday when at a later engagement he said there was no "good" answer to the question of Irish unity.

But far from backtracking he suggested such a scenario would be "cool".

Unionists politicians and the UK government were quick to down play President Trump's "unhelpful" intervention.

They compared it to other rash 'Trumpisims' like taking over Greenland or making Canada the 51st US state.

But unlike those, the conversation around Irish reunification is real and happening and there is a political pathway in the Good Friday Agreement to make it happen.

President Trump's intervention was not a game changer in the move towards Irish reunification.

A border poll is no closer today than it was when Air Force one landed in Dublin yesterday.

But it might feel like a momentum changer for those driving the campaign for Irish unity.

Expect them to continually reference the endorsement of the most powerful man in the world.

Though nothing will change until the UK government decides otherwise as only it has the power to trigger a border poll.

As yet, there is no clear criteria as to what threshold needs to be met.

Donald Trump will be back in the spotlight on Sunday as he watches the closing round of the Irish Open.

Among those in his party is the former DUP MP and Trump family friend Ian Paisley.

He tried to downplay the president's new found love for Irish unity yesterday insisting "everyone was entitled to a personal opinion even if it's wrong".

He will be hoping the president backtracks today when confronted by the media.

The taoiseach will also be in the Trump tent just off the 18th green and will likely be chased by the press pack.

Both leaders will be determined to focus on the golf but questions on Irish unity are now firmly in play.

articles.title: Niger military government reshuffles army command weeks after deadly mutiny
articles.summary: New chief of staff appointed after failed mutiny tested military rulers’ grip on power.
articles.body:
Niger’s military government has named a new chief of the armed forces as it reshuffled its top military command following a failed mutiny late last month.

A decree read on state television on Friday announced that General Mamane Sani Kiaou, previously the army’s chief of staff, would take over as head of the armed forces, replacing General Moussa Salaou Barmou.

Both men had held senior posts since a July 2023 coup brought a group of army officers – led by General Abdourahamane Tchiani – to power.

No reason was given for Barmou’s removal.

General Abdourahmane Abou Zataka has been promoted to succeed Kiaou as army chief of staff, according to the same decree.

Regional broadcaster RFI reported that General Ismael K Sidi Omar has also been named the new second-in-command of the general staff. Sidi Omar previously commanded Base 101, RFI reported, the airport base at the centre of the mutiny, and remained loyal to Tchiani throughout the crisis.

The mutiny that began on August 28 lasted almost 24 hours , drawing in fighting at the presidential palace, Niamey’s international airport and a nearby military base.

Mostly young soldiers took fellow servicemen hostage and opened fire on several sensitive sites, according to Niger’s Ministry of Defence.

Military government forces needed support from Russia’s Africa Corps , a state-backed force that has replaced the mercenary group Wagner in several African countries, which stepped in with ground and air support.

Dozens of mutineers were killed or arrested, along with three members of the presidential guard, though the government has not disclosed an overall death toll or said what charges detained soldiers might face.

Analysts and diplomats told The Associated Press news agency that the mutineers appeared driven by anger over worsening attacks by armed groups and poor conditions within the military.

Kiaou is a field commander who has led operations against armed groups in Niger’s western Tillaberi region and the southeastern Diffa region, and helped negotiate the withdrawal of French and United States troops after the coup.

State media reported he recently completed a tour of the country’s main garrisons intended to restore unity among the ranks.

Tchiani’s government seized power in July 2023 from elected President Mohamed Bazoum, who remains in detention, arguing the civilian government had failed to contain armed groups and violence.

Since then, Niger has cut military ties with France and the US and drawn closer to Russia, even as the security situation has continued to deteriorate.

Niger has accused France of being behind last month’s mutiny, an allegation the French government dismissed as “pure fantasy”.

articles.title: In 2012, UC Davis sank 238 rubber mats across five acres of Lake Tahoe, using them as underwater blankets to suffocate invasive clams and kill about 90% of them
articles.summary: US News: Explore how UC Davis researchers successfully used rubber mats to suffocate invasive Asian clams in Lake Tahoe, achieving a 90% mortality rate without chemicals.
articles.body: Lake Tahoe is known for its clear blue water, but an invasive species had taken hold beneath the surface. Asian clams had spread along parts of the shoreline, competing with native organisms and altering the lakebed. Instead of using chemicals, researchers from UC Davis and their partners covered the clams with thick rubber barriers and cut off their oxygen supply.According to the UC Davis Tahoe Environmental Research Centre, Asian clams (Corbicula fluminea) were first discovered along Lake Tahoe's south shore in 2002. Within several years, the non-native bivalves had reached densities of thousands of clams per square metre in some locations. The clams could affect native invertebrates, benthic habitats and nutrient cycling, and their activity could also add nutrients that encourage algae growth. The problem was particularly concerning in Emerald Bay, where researchers found an isolated population on a shallow gravel sill near the entrance to the bay. Because the population was small and isolated, scientists saw a chance to control it before it became harder to manage.Turning rubber into an underwater barrierResearchers had already tested the idea on a smaller scale. In 2010, scientists from UC Davis and the University of Nevada, Reno covered Asian clam beds at another Lake Tahoe site with artificial rubber sheets to deprive the clams of oxygen. The results were more than 98 per cent mortality after the removal of these sheets, and the density of clams was 90 per cent less than the control area even after one year.Research published in Environmental Management examined the use of gas-impermeable benthic barriers to create oxygen-depleted conditions around Asian clams in Lake Tahoe. The study found that artificially creating anoxic conditions could provide an effective non-chemical method for controlling the invasive bivalves. The Emerald Bay project was far larger. In October 2012, UC Davis scientists prepared 238 rolls of rubber barrier, each 100 feet long and weighing about 300 pounds. The material was reinforced with roughly 10 miles of rebar and 16,000 grommets, while valves were incorporated into the barriers so divers could collect water samples from beneath them without removing the material. The barriers were then readied for placement across about five acres of lakebed in Emerald Bay.The goal was not just to cover the clams. Organic material was placed beneath the barriers to accelerate oxygen depletion, while the rubber sheets prevented oxygen-rich water from reaching the sediment. In effect, the lakebed became a sealed test area. As the oxygen disappeared, the clams were deprived of a condition they needed to survive.What happened beneath the matsThe underwater setting made the larger experiment much harder than the earlier trials. Emerald Bay's entrance experiences strong currents, which could move or overturn the barriers. The lakebed was also made up of porous and uneven glacial material, allowing oxygen-rich water to move through the sediment beneath the barriers. UC Davis therefore had to monitor conditions under the mats rather than assuming that simply covering the clams would be enough.The barriers remained in place far longer than the initial treatment period. Data collection included taking sediment samples as well as monitoring oxygen levels, nutrient loads, and the impact on the clams and other creatures. By the time the physical obstacles were removed in 2014, the project had been carried out on approximately 5.5 acres in Emerald Bay. Preliminary results showed a mortality rate of 90 per cent among the Asian clams. The result did not eliminate the species from Lake Tahoe. The difficult conditions in Emerald Bay allowed some clams to survive, and the larger Lake Tahoe population continues to pose a management problem. According to UC Davis, the Emerald Bay treatment was only one part of a broader strategy.A blanket designed to run out of oxygenThe technique worked because the scientists exploited one of the clams' survival requirements. Instead of adding chemicals to the water, the barriers changed the local microenvironment. By isolating the water from the oxygen-consuming sediment, the area beneath the rubber became less suitable for the clams. However, there was an issue associated with the use of the technique. The treatment affected not only the invasive species but also non-target benthic organisms. Any evaluation of the technique had to consider both its effectiveness against the invaders and its impact on the lakebed ecosystem.This trade-off may have been one of the reasons why this solution was applied to a smaller area with a limited infestation of clams rather than the whole lake. Laying the rubber on the lake bottom was labour-intensive and costly, and it had to withstand currents long enough to create lethal conditions for the clams. The experiment showed that invasive clams can be controlled without chemicals. It looked like a patch of clear water, but beneath the surface hundreds of rolls of rubber were laid on the lakebed, held down, monitored and studied to deprive the clams of oxygen.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: A 30-year-old Canberra father died after allegedly being struck by a semi-trailer on the Federal Highway at Bywong, near Lake George, last week, just three weeks after his family welcomed their newborn daughter.Harsh Sharma, an Indian national who had been living in Canberra with his wife and children for several years, was allegedly hit by the truck on the night of September 3. He died at the scene.According to The Canberra Times, Sharma was a healthcare employee and a father of two young daughters. His family had welcomed their second daughter only three weeks before his death.Harkirat Singh, a childhood friend of Sharma, described the incident as an "incredibly painful" time for the family."Only three weeks earlier, Harsh and his family had welcomed their beautiful newborn daughter into the world. What should have been one of the happiest chapters of their lives has suddenly become a period of unimaginable grief," Singh told The Canberra Times from Sydney."Harsh passed away suddenly and tragically at just 30 years old, leaving behind his loving wife and two beautiful little daughters."Sharma's remains are being prepared for repatriation to his hometown in Punjab, India, where his parents live.Friends in Australia, led by Singh, have launched a crowdfunding campaign to help cover the cost of repatriating Sharma's remains and support his widow and two young children.Emergency services were called to the Federal Highway near Bungendore Road, about 25km northeast of Canberra, at around 9.40pm on September 3."Officers attached to Monaro Police District attended and found a pedestrian had been struck by a semi-trailer truck. The pedestrian, a man believed to be aged in his 30s, died at the scene," a NSW Police spokesperson said.A section of the Federal Highway was closed for several hours as police established a crime scene, with traffic diverted onto the Old Federal Highway.Nick Shelley, 38, who was returning to Sydney from a meeting in Canberra, drove past the crash site minutes after the incident."Yeah, it was a shock to see," Shelley said. "A very large number of cars had pulled over and were rendering assistance to the victim. Several semi-trailers had also pulled over with their hazard lights on. It was a very dark patch of road."Investigators from the Crash Investigation Unit examined the circumstances surrounding the collision. The truck driver, a man in his 30s, was taken to Canberra Hospital for mandatory testing.NSW Police later confirmed that there were no suspicious circumstances surrounding Sharma's death and that no charges had been laid.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
