articles.title: US narrows air protection windows for tankers in Hormuz after surge in Iranian attacks: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: The United States has restricted the hours during which it provides military protection specifically air protection to commercial tankers sailing thro.
articles.body: The United States has restricted the hours during which it provides military protection specifically air protection to commercial tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, after a surge in Iranian attacks on ships using the strategic waterway, according to a Financial Times report.The US has provided air-based protection since May to vessels using a route along the Omani coast on the southern side of the strait, allowing some oil shipments to continue despite Iranian attacks.Under the arrangement, shipowners first sought clearance from the US naval coordination centre, known as Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping (NCAGS), which provided vessels with coordinates and transit windows during which US aircraft would offer protection.But the FT, citing emails sent by NCAGS to maritime advisers, reported that the broad overnight windows were reduced around the start of September to two specified transit slots each day. Ships were encouraged to begin their journeys at designated times to receive the best available US military support.US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, declined to elaborate on the messages, saying the NCAGS communications spoke for themselves.The change came as attacks on commercial shipping intensified. Iran said on Wednesday that it had targeted two US vessels and eight oil tankers in retaliation for US strikes on five Iranian tankers. The US military said those strikes followed an attack by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on an American warship with ballistic missiles.UK Maritime Trade Operations also reported further Iranian attacks on tankers near Dubai and Iraq.More than 70 commercial vessels have been attacked since the conflict began on February 28, according to FT.The southern route has become particularly vulnerable to Iranian surveillance. The IRGC has used small patrol boats to detect merchant ships travelling along the Omani side, many of which have traditionally sailed at night with lights and GPS signals switched off.US support is now being concentrated into shorter windows rather than covering much of the night. Joshua Tallis, a naval analyst at US security research organisation CNA, told the FT that the move could help Washington manage the cost of maintaining a potentially prolonged military presence around the southern route.Tallis estimated that operating an advanced US military aircraft can cost between $25,000 and $75,000 an hour.A maritime security adviser working with ships in the Gulf told the FT that concentrating US aircraft and other resources into shorter periods could allow Washington to provide stronger protection when vessels are transiting.A commercial ship travelling at slow to moderate speed takes about seven hours to cross the strait, meaning the restricted protection windows could require operators to carefully plan their movements.Iran has also announced plans for a “restricted zone” in the Strait of Hormuz. Mohsen Rezaei, head of the country’s Supreme National Security Council, said the zone would extend from the US naval blockade towards the strait and into the Persian Gulf. Tehran said ships entering the zone could face unspecified “sanctions”.At the same time, Iran and Oman have agreed on details of new entry and exit routes for vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with Iranian officials saying the two countries will brief other Gulf states on the arrangement at a regional meeting in Muscat on Monday.However, shipbroker Clarksons does not expect disruption to shipping through the strait to ease until at least the second half of 2027, according to the FT.Retired US Vice Admiral John Miller, who previously commanded American naval forces in the Middle East, said the US would need to conserve its military resources if the protection mission continued for an extended period.Providing air cover around the clock would be difficult to sustain indefinitely, Miller told the FT, making some form of scheduling necessary.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sweden votes as migration, crime and economy dominate high-stakes election
articles.summary: Gun violence, asylum policy and welfare reform dominate Sweden's election as Ulf Kristersson's coalition battles Magdalena Andersson's Social Democrats.
articles.body: Swedes head to the polls Sunday as Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s center-right party is slightly behind the center-left Social Democratic Party led by Sweden's former Prime Minister Magdalena Andersson, with the election dominated by fears of mass migration, crime and the economy. "Years of gang violence, Islamist extremism, persistent unemployment and pressure on public services have intensified the debate over whether integration has kept pace with immigration," foreign policy expert and author Daniel Schatz, told Fox News Digital. DENMARK'S LEFT-WING PM WARNS: 'BIG ENEMY HAS STARTED TO GROW FROM WITHIN' AS EUROPE FACES MIGRANT RECKONING Following on from Germany's AfD victory in a state election last week, Sweden's hard-right Sweden Democrats are in a position to enter government if Kristersson's party wins again. The Associated Press reported that the anti-immigration party has shifted toward the political mainstream and is likely to get cabinet posts. It has so far supported the Kristersson government from the outside. The Associated Press reported that the Sweden Democrats were founded by activists in far-right-wing extremist groups, including neo-Nazis. But since then, under its leader, Jimmie Åkesson, it toned down that rhetoric and kicked out racist members. Åkesson, who has led them since 2005, is said to be responsible for the success of a once marginal party. Sweden, once a model of the Western social welfare state, has been under economic strain as governments from both the left and the right were forced to restructure their welfare system. While social benefits continue to be extensive, Sweden’s welfare state has changed amid rising crime rates, but the expectations for public benefits remain. "Sweden went from being described as a ‘humanitarian superpower’ to a "humanitarian basket case.’ Discontent with migration policies extends to both foreign-born and native-born residents. Shootings have declined sharply, but fewer shootings do not mean the integration problems are solved," Schatz, who is Swedish, added. Prime Minister Kristersson’s government took power in 2022, as the nation was experiencing a dramatic rise in gun-related violence, with the country witnessing 391 shootings resulting in 62 deaths, according to The Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention, a government agency under the Ministry of Justice. SWEDEN JAMS SUSPECTED RUSSIAN DRONE NEAR FRENCH CARRIER AS NATO WAR FEARS RISE The homicide rate in Sweden has been on the rise since 2013, when gun homicides contributed to a general increase in Sweden’s total homicide rate. The Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention notes that Sweden’s homicide rate ranks very high compared with other European countries, at approximately four deaths per million inhabitants per year. The average for Europe is approximately 1.6 deaths per million inhabitants. The issue of immigration is another major issue that dovetails with voters’ concerns over crime and gun violence. Like much of Europe, Sweden experienced a wave of immigration in 2015 coming from those fleeing the Syrian civil war as well as the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Sweden took in over 160,000 asylum seekers in 2015, or 12% of all those who sought protection in the EU, according to Sweden’s Migration Agency. "After the 2015 influx of asylum seekers from Syria and other war-torn countries strained its reception system, Sweden began tightening its borders. The current government has taken that shift much further," Schatz said. ANTI-MIGRANT AFD SEEKS TO BREAK GERMANY’S POLITICAL ‘FIREWALL’ IN HISTORIC STATE ELECTION Prime Minister Kristersson’s parliamentary ally, the right-wing Sweden Democrats, filled the void in the anti-immigration position in parliament. Nicholas Aylott, professor of political science at Södertörn University in Stockholm, told Fox News Digital that the link between the increase in immigration and the rise in crime changed Swedish politics. "Migration and law-and-order became much higher electoral priorities," Aylott said. "The Sweden Democrats based their pitch on them. The other parties, rather belatedly, adapted their positions. The Sweden Democrats had at first been completely ostracized by the other parties, but they were gradually accepted as a legitimate partner by three of the other parties of the right between 2018 and 2022," he said. As the anti-immigration backlash rose and the Sweden Democrats were more included in the policymaking process, Sweden cracked down on immigration and made it harder to seek asylum. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Southern breakfast chain in just 3 states beats McDonald's, Chick-fil-A for best in America
articles.summary: With just 90 locations in three states, Biscuitville outranked Chick-fil-A and McDonald's as America's best fast-food breakfast for a fourth straight year.
articles.body: For the fourth year in a row, Biscuitville has claimed the title of America's best fast-food breakfast, beating out national chains despite a footprint that remains concentrated in just three states. The Southern breakfast chain earned the top spot in USA Today's 10Best Readers' Choice Awards, beating out larger chains like McDonald's (No. 4), Chick-fil-A (No. 5), Burger King (No. 6) and Wendy's (No. 7). Kristie Mitchell, Biscuitville's chief marketing officer, said the recognition is particularly meaningful because of the competition in the fast-food breakfast category. AMERICA'S FAVORITE FAST-FOOD CHAIN NAMED: MCDONALD'S WINS HEARTS BUT NOT BEST BURGER, SURVEY SAYS "We have earned it, but we don't want to live in a space where we come to expect it," Mitchell said. Biscuitville recently opened its 90th restaurant and currently operates in North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia. Mitchell said Biscuitville eventually hopes to expand into states such as Tennessee and Georgia, though the family-owned company plans to focus on growing within its existing markets for the next several years. Biscuitville's calling card remains its scratch-made biscuits, prepared fresh every 15 minutes from a three-ingredient family recipe that Mitchell said was passed down to the company's founder by his grandmother. FAST-FOOD GIANT DETHRONED AS CUSTOMER STUDY CROWNS AMERICA'S NEW FAVORITE RESTAURANT CHAIN But Biscuitville's appeal, Mitchell argues, goes beyond the biscuit. "We have no microwaves," she said. "There's no instant anything in our kitchens." Eggs are hand-cracked, and Mitchell said nothing arrives at the restaurants partially cooked simply to be finished there. The approach requires more planning and labor, particularly when customers still expect the speed of a drive-thru window. The result, Mitchell believes, taps into something larger than convenience. Celebrity chef Jason Smith, who is a contestant on the upcoming season of Fox's "The Floor," agrees that Biscuitville belongs among the country's breakfast heavyweights. "Do I agree it's the best breakfast biscuit sandwich I've ever had?" he told Fox News Digital. "Well, no, but it would come in a high second on my list." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS His complaint comes down to one ingredient: butter. "That's what makes the best Southern biscuits," the Kentucky-born chef said. Smith instead gives his personal top spot to Tudor's Biscuit World, a regional chain with locations including West Virginia, Kentucky and Ohio. Still, he praised Biscuitville's biscuits as tender and "super soft" and singled out its Ultimate Country Ham Biscuit as a favorite. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ For Mitchell, the enduring popularity of biscuits, grits, eggs and other Southern breakfast staples comes back to an experience that can resonate even with people who didn't grow up eating them. "I think it's bigger than just the biscuit," she said. "Yes, we are Biscuitville, but it's bigger than just the biscuit. It's all the things that go between that biscuit." articles.body: An Indian-origin laboratory owner has been placed on the US federal fugitive list after authorities accused him of engaging in a USD 93 million Medicare fraud scheme involving genetic testing.Khadeer Khan Mohammed, 46, allegedly used his Texas-based laboratory to submit fraudulent claims to Medicare, a US government-funded healthcare programme. Authorities allege that the scheme involved genetic tests that were not eligible for reimbursement, were not ordered by authorised doctors and were not used in patient care.$93 million in claims, $65 million paidAccording to the US Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG), Mohammed owned American Premier Labs LLC in Richardson, Texas.Between August 2023 and October 2024, Mohammed allegedly submitted, or directed others to submit, around $93 million in fraudulent Medicare claims through the laboratory. Medicare paid at least $65 million on those claims, authorities said.In one 10-day period in 2023, Medicare allegedly paid about $13 million towards the claims.Doctors' identities allegedly misusedA key part of the alleged scheme involved the use of physicians' personal identifying information without their knowledge or consent.According to HHS-OIG, claims were submitted for genetic tests for Medicare beneficiaries whose doctors had no treatment relationship with them. The physicians allegedly did not order the tests and the results were not used in treating the beneficiaries.Authorities allege the doctors' identities were used to make the laboratory claims appear medically authorised.Mohammed may be in HyderabadUS authorities have now listed Mohammed as a fugitive and said he may be in Hyderabad, India.The case was investigated by the FBI's Dallas Field Office and HHS-OIG. Prosecutors from the US Attorney's Office for the Northern District of Texas are handling the criminal case.Authorities have also reportedly seized nearly $6 million from bank accounts allegedly controlled by Mohammed.Anyone with information about his whereabouts has been asked to contact the HHS-OIG fugitive hotline at 888-476-4453 or submit a fugitive sighting report.The allegations against Mohammed have not been proven in court. articles.title: Old planes and no money: Pakistan's air force is about to go into a nosedive
articles.summary: International News: Air forces around the world have been shrinking in size since the end of the Cold War, although not necessarily in capability. The Indian Air Force (I.
articles.body: Air forces around the world have been shrinking in size since the end of the Cold War, although not necessarily in capability. The Indian Air Force (IAF), for instance, has a sanctioned strength of 42.5 squadrons but now operates fewer than 30. Its fleet peaked at around 40 squadrons in 1996, according to the New Delhi-based Council for Strategic and Defense Research.India is hardly an outlier. The United States, which has by far the world's largest defence budget, had a tactical fighter fleet of around 4,500 aircraft at the end of the Cold War. That number has since fallen to less than half, according to the official publication Air & Space Forces Magazine. The Royal Air Force and most other air forces, particularly in the Western world, have experienced similar declines.China, however, has been the major exception, expanding its air force in both numbers and capability over the same period.One of the primary reasons for the decline is what came to be known as the "peace dividend". With the threat of a major conventional war appearing to recede after the collapse of the Soviet Union, many countries cut defence spending and, consequently, reduced the size of their armed forces.Europe benefited from this peace dividend for decades, until Russia's invasion of Ukraine fundamentally changed the continent's security calculations. The war, coupled with US President Donald Trump's pressure on European allies to shoulder more of the burden for their own defence, has pushed European countries to strengthen their military capabilities.Nato members have now committed to significantly higher defence spending, with the alliance setting a new target of up to 5% of GDP. Countries such as Latvia and Poland are already at or approaching that level, while others are working to rapidly rebuild their military capabilities in response to the perceived threat from Russia.There is, however, another factor behind the shrinking size of fighter fleets, and one that affects countries far more broadly: the rising cost of buying and maintaining modern combat aircraft, even after accounting for inflation.In most countries, procuring fighter aircraft — arguably the most expensive and technologically sophisticated machines in any military — is subject to intense political and financial scrutiny. Maintaining a modern fighter fleet is therefore as much a function of politics and economics as it is of military requirements.The cost is difficult to avoid. Modern fighters are vastly more capable than their predecessors were in 1990. They can detect threats at greater distances, engage targets farther away, strike with far greater accuracy, operate as part of sophisticated networks and provide pilots with vastly greater situational awareness. But all of that capability comes at a price. As fighter aircraft become more capable, each individual aircraft also becomes dramatically more expensive to buy, operate and maintain.Pakistan bucks the trendIslamabad has gone to considerable lengths to maintain the numerical strength of its combat fleet, both by inducting new aircraft and by upgrading older airframes.Its Mirage fleet is perhaps the clearest example. The Mirage III and Mirage V, once among the world's most widely used fighter aircraft, have long since been retired by virtually all their former operators. Pakistan, however, continues to operate them.The Pakistan Air Force (PAF) operates a diverse fighter fleet sourced from France, the United States and, increasingly, China.Its inventory includes the American F-16, the French-origin Mirage III and Mirage V, and a growing number of Chinese-origin aircraft. The latter include the F-7 and J-10, as well as the JF-17, which Pakistan assembles domestically in cooperation with China.The last PAF F-7 squadron is now transitioning to the JF-17 Block III. Once that transition is complete, the number of JF-17-equipped squadrons will rise from six to seven.The PAF also operates three F-16 squadrons. Two of these were inducted in the 1980s, while the third was inducted around 2010. In addition, there are four squadrons operating Mirage III and Mirage V fighters. Pakistan began inducting the Mirage in 1967, with some aircraft subsequently acquired from Saudi Arabia and others obtained second-hand from the Royal Australian Air Force.The newest addition to the fleet is the Chinese J-10CE, which Pakistan has recently acquired.This creates a significant challenge for the PAF. Six of its fighter squadrons (two F-16 squadrons and four Mirage squadrons) will need replacement over the coming years. In a force of around 15 frontline fighter squadrons, losing six represents roughly 40% of the fleet, making this a potentially significant capability gap.The PAF's total fighter-related strength is larger when training and conversion units are included. It has a fighter squadron each of F-16s, JF-17s and Mirages at the Combat Commanders' School (CCS), the PAF's equivalent of the US Navy's Top Gun school or the IAF's Tactics and Combat Development Establishment. It also operates four operational conversion units flying F-16s and JF-17s.Taken together, these formations bring the number of PAF squadrons operating fighter aircraft to around 22. Beyond these are combat-support units performing critical missions, including airborne early warning, electronic warfare and other specialised roles.For decades, Pakistan has sought to maintain a degree of numerical parity with India, and it has gone to considerable lengths to preserve the size of its combat fleet. But it is now staring at what could be a significant gap.The problem is particularly acute because much of the older fleet is approaching the end of its Technical Total Life (TTL). Pakistan's Mirage fleet is extremely old, while some of its F-16s are also approaching the limits of their service lives.The PAF's last publicly announced major order for its "indigenous" fighter came in 2020, when it ordered 50 airframes of the advanced JF-17 Block III. Pakistan has also received the last of its 20 J-10 fighters, according to the International Institute for Strategic Studies.Based on publicly announced orders, therefore, the PAF appears to be facing a significant decline in numbers unless it secures another major fighter procurement programme.Pakistan has been seeking China's fifth-generation J-35 fighter, but no formal deal has yet been announced. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif had also posted a list of military equipment that Pakistan was expected to procure from China on social media, but the post was subsequently deleted, adding to speculation over a possible deal.Pakistan has already demonstrated its willingness to spend heavily on military hardware.It was the world's fifth-largest recipient of major arms in 2021–25, up from 10th place in 2016–20, with its arms imports increasing by 66% between the two periods. Pakistan accounted for 4.2% of global arms imports during 2021–25, and 80% of those imports came from China, up from 73% in 2016–20.The bigger question is whether Pakistan can afford to maintain this pace.With a struggling economy and a substantial debt burden, financing an entirely new generation of fighters will be difficult. Pakistan has the world's 40th-largest economy, according to the IMF, yet it maintains what is ranked as the world's seventh-largest air force.The contrast with Bangladesh is revealing. Bangladesh is economically better placed than Pakistan but has a much smaller air force, ranked 65th by a major military tracker. The comparison illustrates the extraordinary importance Pakistan has placed on maintaining a large combat fleet.But there may be a limit to how long Islamabad can sustain that ambition.To paraphrase the original Top Gun, the PAF may be writing cheques that the Pakistani economy cannot cash.This is not entirely unprecedented. Pakistan's former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto famously declared that the country would "eat grass" if necessary to acquire a nuclear weapon. Today, Islamabad faces a similar scenario: with an economy that is nosediving, how much is it willing to sacrifice to maintain the world's seventh-largest air force?

articles.title: Wisconsin Rep. Tom Tiffany says he sustained minor injuries as plane makes emergency landing on lake
articles.summary: Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for Wisconsin governor, says he sustained minor injuries late Saturday when a plane he was traveling in was forced to make an emergency water landing.
articles.body: Rep. Tom Tiffany, the Republican nominee for Wisconsin governor, says he sustained minor injuries late Saturday when a plane he was traveling in was forced to make an emergency water landing. Tiffany said in a statement on X that he and the pilot swam to safety after the light aircraft, which had lost power while approaching Wisconsin’s Wausau Downtown Airport, landed in Lake Wausau and began to submerge. “I want to express my deepest gratitude to the pilot, the Wausau Fire Department, and all of the first responders who came to our aid so quickly,” Tiffany said. “They got us safely off the water and transported us to Aspirus Wausau Hospital, where we received excellent care. Thankfully, both the pilot and I sustained only minor injuries.” Rescue teams were called to reports of a downed plane with two people in the water, emergency services’ radio communications obtained by NBC News indicate. Two survivors pulled out of the water were “alert and conscious,” the audio suggests. Tiffany represents ⁠Wisconsin’s seventh congressional district and is endorsed by President Donald Trump in the November 3 gubernatorial election. His Democratic opponent, David Crowley, said in a post on X: “I’m grateful to God that Congressman Tiffany and no one else was hurt in this horrifying incident, which could have been a tragedy if not for the heroism of the pilot.” He added: “I wish them and the Congressman a quick recovery and that they can find solace with their loved ones.” “An experience like this reminds you just how precious life is,” Tiffany said in his post.

articles.title: Man charged with concealing identity at Portsmouth protest
articles.summary: Anti-migrant demonstrators marched in Portsmouth on Saturday, and a counter-protest was also held.
articles.body:
A man has been charged with concealing his identity at a protest in Portsmouth, after police warned they would arrest demonstrators using face masks and coverings.

Several hundred anti-migrant protesters marched through the city centre while anti-racism groups also made their way to Guildhall Square on Saturday.

Hampshire Police said Timothy Miller, 76, of Sherwood Avenue in Hedge End was charged with wearing or using an item to conceal identity at a protest. He is due before Portsmouth magistrates on Monday.

David McNally, 33, of Winchester Road in Portsmouth, was also charged with obstructing the highway and attempted criminal damage. He is due in court on 29 October.

Hampshire Police said on Friday it would use new powers under the Crime and Policing Act to prevent protesters wearing face coverings that conceal their identity.

Both sets of demonstrators were kept apart by police when they arrived at Guldhall Square.

The city centre protests followed disorder on 6 September when police attended Eastney Marina as hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

A 16-year-old male from Waterlooville was also arrested at Saturday's protests on suspicion of violent disorder, in relation to the events at Eastney Marina.

He has been released on bail until 12 December.

Del Leon Somerville, 42, from Paulsgrove appeared at Portsmouth Magistrates Court on Saturday charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police officer at the Eastney protest.

He was remanded in custody to appear at Portsmouth Crown Court on 16 September.

articles.title: Fighting continues between Yemen gov’t forces, Houthis: What is the latest?
articles.summary: Government forces and Saudi Arabia carry out air attacks to stop Houthis’ advance as thousands displaced by conflict.
articles.body:
Fighting has intensified on several fronts in Yemen as the government forces have carried out air attacks on Houthi positions in attempts to retake Mocha, days after the Iran-backed group captured the strategic port city, tightening its grip on the Red Sea – a vital shipping lane.

The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (supporters of God), have accused Saudi Arabia of launching more than 100 air attacks on Yemen within the past 48 hours.

Saudi Arabia backs the internationally recognised government, which has described the latest fighting as a “battle for survival”.

The fighting has forced tens of thousands of Yemenis from their homes, including more than 2,000 who headed to Djibouti.

What is the latest situation on the ground? What is the Saudi role in the conflict, and how has Iran responded?

What is the latest situation on the ground?

On Saturday, Yemeni government forces said they had launched air attacks on Houthi fighters along the Red Sea coast after the group seized full control of the strategic shoreline.

Yemen’s government news agency, Saba, reported that “the armed forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia backed by the Iranian regime” near the port city of Mocha.

The spokesperson for the government forces, Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, said they also struck the Houthis’ “vehicles and members” on the Mocha-Dhubab road, 11km (7 miles) from the city, according to Saba.

The government’s attacks came after the Houthis captured Mocha on Thursday and the island of Mayyun (also known as Perim) on Friday, completing their hold on the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a narrow waterway vital to global oil shipping.

On Sunday, Sultan al-Arada, a member of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) and governor of Marib, said government forces that withdrew from the west coast are currently regrouping in Marib and will return to the battlefield.

In an interview with state-run Saba TV, al-Arada described what happened on the coast as “painful and unfortunate”, but said such setbacks were part of the nature of war.

Al-Arada accused the Houthis of bringing the peace process to a dead end and “forcing the option of war” back on Yemen.

He said government forces were continuing to fight on several fronts and that the ultimate objective in Marib and elsewhere remained “the restoration of the capital, Sanaa”.

“The forces that withdrew are now rearranging themselves, and they will return to the battle again in one form or another,” he said.

The Yemeni military’s reserve Nation Shield Force also claimed on Sunday that the reserve’s 6th Brigade had downed five drones during clashes in the al-Aghbara area, according to a report by Turkish state-run Anadolu news agency.

Separately, the September Net website, which is affiliated with the army of the internationally recognised Yemeni government, reported that air forces conducted a series of air raids against Houthi targets across the country, saying equipment had been destroyed and Houthi fighters killed, but gave no further details on the number of casualties.

Reporting from Sanaa, Yemen, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry said the government forces are trying to recapture territory near the key city of Mocha from the Houthis.

The Al Jazeera correspondent said Saudi Arabia is carrying out air attacks, mainly against Houthi military advances.

“There have been 129 air strikes on the areas that have recently fallen to the Ansar Allah, including areas in the north where the Houthi group is trying to make advances into the city of Marib, a Yemeni government stronghold.”

Mawry said Houthi military buildups in Taiz have also been hit.

He added that there are also reports of clashes on the outskirts of Marib, a government-held city considered to be the economic hub of Yemen. “Whoever controls it, controls Yemen’s revenue stream,” he said.

Mohammed al-Basha, founder and lead analyst of the Basha Report Risk Advisory, told Al Jazeera that political infighting and division within the government forces are stymying the fight against the fast-moving Houthis.

“You’re not going to be able to defeat the Houthis with a split command and control with eight armies sort of competing over influence,” he said.

He blamed infighting among government forces as a reason for the Houthis’ military gains. “They’re finger-pointing and blaming each other,” he added.

Which are the main front lines in Yemen?

The primary active front lines in the latest escalation involve intense fighting between the Iran-backed group and forces aligned with the internationally recognised Yemeni government. These include:

The western coast and Bab al-Mandeb strait: Intense clashes have focused on the coastal areas, including Mocha and Hodeidah, as Houthi forces push towards vital shipping lanes and chokepoints overlooking the Red Sea.

Taiz: Heavy ground battles and counterattacks have taken place in recent days through the mountainous terrain of Taiz province, which acts as a crucial gateway connecting inland areas to the coast.

Marib and al-Jawf: Over the past few weeks, government forces have been battling to defend and expand their control around Marib and the neighbouring northern governorate of al-Jawf bordering Saudi Arabia.

Dhalea: Acting as a vital territorial connector between the Houthi-controlled north and the south, Dhalea remains a volatile and active line of contact.

What do we know about the latest humanitarian situation in Yemen?

The United Nations said on Friday that nearly 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since fighting escalated earlier this week, though the figure is likely higher, according to Abdusattor Esoev, chief of the International Organization for Migration in Yemen.

Esoev told Al Jazeera that the fall of Mocha, where the UN maintained a strong presence, had made it more difficult for aid agencies to reach people in need.

More than 2,000 Yemenis have arrived in Djibouti in the past 24 hours amid fierce fighting, with at least 76,000 people displaced since July.

What to know about the fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia?

The Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks on southern Saudi Arabia in recent days.

On Tuesday, the group struck civilian and economic facilities in the Saudi cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, wounding 73 people, including women and children.

The attacks on the kingdom are part of a rapid escalation in Yemen’s long-running conflict, which reignited in July after roughly four years of relative calm under a UN-brokered truce.

On Sunday, the Houthis also claimed they had struck a Saudi military base in Sharurah, in the southern Najran province, using ballistic missiles and drones.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X that the attack hit “weapons depots and command and control centres” and that the targeted sites were “managing the aggression against our nation and people”.

Saree, who did not state when the attack took place, warned Saudi Arabia that further military actions would prompt larger, more intense attacks deeper inside Saudi territory.

Earlier, Saree had said that Saudi warplanes had launched 129 air raids over the past 48 hours, “targeting the governorates of Taiz, Marib, Hodeidah, al-Jawf, Saada, Amran, and Hajjah”.

He added that F-15 and Typhoon aircraft were used in the attacks and took off from bases in Saudi Arabia’s Khamis Mushait and Taif.

“These attacks on our people will not go unanswered, God willing,” he added.

On Sunday, Saudi Civil Defence said two people were wounded and a mosque and several buildings were damaged after a projectile fired by the Houthi fighters struck Saudi Arabia’s southern Jazan region.

Several vehicles were also damaged by the projectile that landed in Jazan’s al-Tuwal governorate on Saturday, it added.

A Civil Defence spokesperson called the attacks on civilian objects a “flagrant violation of international humanitarian law”, adding that established emergency procedures had been implemented.

Al-Basha, the analyst, told Al Jazeera that Saudi Arabia is facing growing pressure to launch a larger military operation against the Houthis, but any campaign would still depend heavily on forces fighting on the ground.

He noted that while the Saudi-led coalition has not officially acknowledged carrying out air attacks, “it’s safe to say that the Saudis are providing air support.”

But he said air power alone would not be enough.

“Aircraft and firepower could suppress, could slow down the advance of the Houthis, but it’s the forces on the ground that will make a difference,” he said.

Al-Basha said he also did not expect the United States to join the fighting directly.

“We are not at war with the Houthis. The Houthis are not at war with us,” he said, referring to the US position, adding that Washington could still support any future Saudi operation with “intelligence, refuelling, logistics and military advice”.

But he added that “the Houthis will do whatever they can do to take over the whole of the country.”

Al-Basha said he did not expect either side to collapse quickly, predicting instead “a protracted conflict” more similar to Sudan, with both sides eventually forced to negotiate.

Iranian authorities and state media have praised the Houthis’ capture of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, which some see as giving Tehran more leverage against the US.

“The victories of Yemen’s Ansar Allah in the western coast is a narrative of a divine triumph and the fruit of years of steadfastness in the most difficult of battlefields,” Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), wrote on X on Saturday.

Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iranian parliament speaker, reposted a comment made by slain Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in 2024, saying the “resistance” of the Houthis will inevitably lead to victory.

“The brave Yemeni people will certainly triumph, by permission of God Almighty,” Ghalibaf added on Thursday, in Arabic.

The “grand victory” of the Houthis once again proved that “security is not a commodity that can be bought,” added Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.

But Iran’s diplomatic apparatus did not immediately link the Houthi advances with the current fight against the US.

As has often been the case, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs insisted that the Houthis make their decisions independent of Tehran, with their own interests at heart, including ending Saudi Arabia’s blockade on Yemen.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry also called for an end to the Saudi siege on Houthi-controlled areas, an immediate return to negotiations between the group and Riyadh, and respect for Yemen’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The ministry pushed back on the idea that the Houthis act merely as a proxy for Tehran.

“What is happening now in Yemen is the result of the Yemenis losing patience,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told state television on Friday night.

“It is not fair to ignore the fact that they were under a cruel blockade for years, and concluded that the United Nations and regional mechanisms could not resolve the issues.”

Yemen’s more than a decade-long civil war has flared up once again after the Houthi armed group launched an offensive in several locations against Saudi-backed government forces earlier this month. The conflict has already spilled over beyond the country’s borders, with the Houthis carrying out attacks in southern Saudi Arabia, including oil facilities. Dozens of people were wounded in those attacks.

The renewed hostilities are the most serious since a UN-brokered truce halted large-scale fighting in 2022, after eight years of a full-blown conflict that killed tens of thousands of people in one of the world’s poorest countries.

The Houthis took over vast swaths of Yemen in 2014. Months later, Saudi Arabia intervened militarily in support of the internationally backed government.

The Iran-backed group continues to control northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa. It is seen as part of a regional alliance known as the “axis of resistance” backed by Iran. The group nevertheless has its own base, its own interests – and its own ambitions.

The PLC was established in 2022 when the former president, Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi, formally transferred his powers to the new eight-member body. It represents the internationally recognised government of Yemen.

Its membership is drawn from a mix of northern and southern politicians and military-linked leaders in a bid to unite major anti-Houthi forces under one roof.

The PLC is backed by Saudi Arabia and the alliance that Riyadh leads.

The Yemeni Congregation for Reform, better known as Islah, is a Sunni Islamist movement with historic ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. It is a faction within the recognised PLC-led government but has long had an independent identity. Its major stronghold has long been Marib, the country’s sole gas-producing region with one of its largest oilfields.

The National Resistance Forces is a government-aligned military faction led by Tareq Saleh, nephew of the late former President Ali Abdullah Saleh.

The force has maintained ties to Saudi Arabia and, like the Islah party, is part of the PLC. It aims for a unified Yemen, positioning itself as a counterweight to both the Houthis and southern secessionists.

Riyadh entered the Yemen war when it led a military coalition against the Houthis in March 2015, seeking to restore the government of then-President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi. Back then, Saudi Arabia and Iran were at the peak of a regional competition, both deeply distrusting each other. Saudi Arabia saw the control of its southern border by the Iran-aligned Houthis as a security threat.

This was before a China-brokered rapprochement between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023.

articles.title: Parkinson's is becoming more common. Here are 5 things everyone should know
articles.summary: A Parkinson's physician and scientist urges exercise, heart-healthy habits, and social interaction to slow Parkinson's disease as gene therapy research advances.
articles.body: It’s true. Rates of Parkinson’s disease are growing faster than any other neurological condition in the world, with incidence projected to double in the coming decades. Parkinson’s is a progressive disorder that affects the brain, nervous system, and muscle control. As singer-songwriter Carly Simon, who recently announced her Parkinson’s diagnosis, said, this condition is "not a blessing or a gift." I understand. As a physician and scientist specializing in Parkinson’s for over 20 years, I’ve seen its impact on patients and their families. Currently there is no cure for Parkinson’s, and while pills and other symptomatic therapies are helpful, eventually the disease worsens over time. The sobering truth is Parkinson’s changes lives. The greatest fear among those without the disease is the loss of physical independence of their loved ones, and those living with the disease fear its progression and what challenges each new day might bring. CARLY SIMON REVEALS THE COMMON CONDITION THAT MASKED HER PARKINSON'S DIAGNOSIS Knowledge can be a powerful antidote to fear. When it comes to brain health, however, while there’s interest, there are gaps. The Dana Foundation reported that brain health is a top priority for Americans, but 66% report having little or no knowledge about brain health research, with older Americans reporting the lowest levels of knowledge. Better understanding of Parkinson’s removes the mystery, may help people concerned about or currently living with it create a plan, and provides reason for all to believe there could be a better future for those who receive a diagnosis. Here are five points to provide clarity, prompt action, and give hope. Parkinson’s changes lives. The greatest fear among those without the disease is the loss of physical independence of their loved ones, and those living with the disease fear its progression and what challenges each new day might bring. Get moving, every day. Whether or not you have Parkinson’s, regular exercise promotes brain health. For those with the disease, at least 2.5 hours of consistent exercise per week can slow symptom progression and improve physical and emotional well-being. Studies also show that high levels of regular physical activity are strongly associated with a better clinical course of disease. What kinds of exercise are best? Anything that gets you off the couch. Some of my patients have taken up boxing and dance. SIMPLE BODY MOVEMENT COULD HELP THE BRAIN 'CLEAN ITSELF,' RESEARCHERS FIND Be heart-healthy. What is good for the heart is also good for brain health. Heart-healthy habits such as a well-balanced diet, quality sleep, and not smoking are part of healthy living that keeps the heart strong and protects the small blood vessels that supply blood and oxygen to the energy-hungry brain cells. Stay involved. I’ve seen Parkinson’s unlock new artistic skills and interests. Find projects that keep you interacting with others and demand mental effort—important for everyone and critical for those with Parkinson’s. Social interaction and engagement may help maintain daily function, contribute to brain health, and improve overall well-being. LONELINESS MAY BE SILENTLY ERODING YOUR MEMORY, NEW RESEARCH REVEALS Consider sharing your diagnosis if you have been told you have Parkinson’s disease. This is a very personal decision. Research shows some stay silent about Parkinson’s, citing concerns about discrimination at work, stigma, or losing their dignity. Silence can be isolating. Conversely, sharing the diagnosis can deepen bonds with family and friends. I’ve seen families get closer and my patients’ friends really rally, offering daily walks, games, classes, and get-togethers. The Michael J. Fox Foundation provides support for those interested in discussing their disease openly. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Know that strides are being made to find new ways to tackle the biology of Parkinson’s, possibilities that were previously beyond reach. The development of an investigational gene therapy I’m involved with, for example, is aimed at stopping the clock on disease progression, with a goal of helping patients maintain or improve their Parkinson’s motor symptoms so that daily life and activities are minimally disrupted, compared with later-stage symptoms. Scientists in academia and industry are advancing molecular neuroscience, gene delivery, imaging, and biomarkers. While these efforts haven’t yet simplified the complexity and unpredictability of Parkinson’s, there is reason to hope we’ll see advances in Parkinson’s care that go beyond symptom management. As a doctor, Parkinson’s disease is humbling. My patients want more from Parkinson’s medicines and a different future after diagnosis. I do, too. articles.title: 'AAP will be extra cautious': Kejriwal on future Rajya Sabha picks after Raghav Chadha exit
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Aam Aadmi Party supremo Arvind Kejriwal on Sunday said he would be \"extra cautious\" while choosing the party's Rajya Sabha nominees in the .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Aam Aadmi Party supremo Arvind Kejriwal on Sunday said he would be "extra cautious" while choosing the party's Rajya Sabha nominees in the future, referring to instances of its MPs leaving the party.Addressing a public gathering in poll-bound Goa, the former Delhi chief minister said, "AAP will be extra cautious while picking its Rajya Sabha nominees in future, following instances of its MPs leaving the party."Kejriwal's remarks come months after a major setback for AAP in the Rajya Sabha, with several of its MPs rebelling against the party leadership.Raghav Chadha, along with six other Rajya Sabha members, joined the BJP, significantly reducing AAP's strength and voice in Parliament.The Kejriwal-led party is preparing for next year's Goa assembly polls and has also announced a pre-poll alliance with the Goa Forward Party.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
